questionBank.question: On computed tomography (CT), how is white matter depicted in relation to grey matter?

options.label: A
options.text: White matter is lighter than grey matter due to its high water content.

options.label: B
options.text: White matter is darker grey than grey matter due to the radiolucent lipid in myelin.

options.label: C
options.text: White matter appears as a signal void (black) due to a lack of free protons.

options.label: D
options.text: White matter and grey matter are indistinguishable without intravenous contrast.

questionBank.answer: White matter is darker grey than grey matter due to the radiolucent lipid in myelin.
questionBank.explanation: With CT, somewhat paradoxically, white matter is depicted as darker grey than grey matter because white matter contains lipid as part of myelin, which is relatively radiolucent[cite: 10].

questionBank.question: Which of the following best describes the appearance of dense bone on MRI?

options.label: D
options.text: Hyperintense on T1W, hypointense on T2W

questionBank.explanation: Dense bone contains few free protons on which MRI is based and therefore appears as a signal void (black) on MR[cite: 10].

questionBank.question: The frontal bone forms in two halves during development. At what age does the intervening metopic suture normally fuse?
questionBank.explanation: The frontal bone forms in two halves, which normally fuse at five years. The intervening suture is known as the metopic suture[cite: 12].

questionBank.question: The pterion is the junction where the frontal, sphenoid, parietal, and temporal bones meet. When does this normally close?
questionBank.explanation: The frontal, sphenoid parietal and temporal bones meet at the pterion, which normally closes at 3-4 months[cite: 12].

questionBank.question: Which structures are transmitted by the foramen ovale?

options.label: A
options.text: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve and middle meningeal artery

options.label: B
options.text: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and accessory meningeal arteries

questionBank.answer: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and accessory meningeal arteries
questionBank.explanation: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and the accessory meningeal arteries[cite: 12].

questionBank.question: Which inconstant foramen is located medial to the foramen ovale and transmits an emissary vein?
questionBank.explanation: The foramen of Vesalius transmits an emissary vein and is medial to the foramen ovale[cite: 13].

questionBank.question: At approximately what age does the clivus transition from being hypointense to hyperintense on T1W MR images due to fatty marrow replacement?
questionBank.explanation: In the adult the clivus is hyperintense on T1W MR images due to replacement of red marrow with fat. The transition from hypointensity occurs at around 7 years[cite: 14].

questionBank.question: During which age range are convolutional markings on a skull radiograph most prominent?
questionBank.explanation: Convolutional markings are absent at birth, most prominent at between 2 and 5 years and absent after about 12 years[cite: 14].

questionBank.question: Which two structures lie directly above the free edge of the tentorium and are at risk of compression during raised supratentorial intracranial pressure?

options.label: A
options.text: The cerebellar tonsils and the vertebral arteries

options.label: B
options.text: The uncus of the hippocampus and the posterior cerebral arteries

options.label: C
options.text: The pineal gland and the internal cerebral veins

options.label: D
options.text: The oculomotor nerves and the superior cerebellar arteries

questionBank.answer: The uncus of the hippocampus and the posterior cerebral arteries
questionBank.explanation: The uncus of the hippocampus and the posterior cerebral arteries lie above the free edge of the tentorium and both are at risk of compression against the tentorial edge when there is raised intracranial pressure[cite: 15].

questionBank.question: Which cranial ganglia receive arterial supply directly from branches of the middle meningeal arteries?
questionBank.explanation: The middle meningeal arteries supply branches to both the trigeminal and the facial ganglia[cite: 17].

questionBank.question: Which of the following provides the primary sensory innervation to the cranial dura?
questionBank.explanation: Innervation of the dura is primarily from the trigeminal nerve, but also from the lower cranial nerves and the first three cervical segments[cite: 17].

questionBank.question: Which cranial nerves are located within the lateral parts of the cisterna magna alongside the vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries?

options.label: C
options.text: Glossopharyngeal, vagus, and spinal accessory nerves

questionBank.answer: Glossopharyngeal, vagus, and spinal accessory nerves
questionBank.explanation: The vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries travel through the lateral parts of the cisterna magna, which also contains the glossopharyngeal, vagus and spinal accessory nerves[cite: 17].

questionBank.question: Which cistern contains the circle of Willis?
questionBank.explanation: The chiasmatic or suprasellar cistern extends from the infundibulum to the posterior surface of the frontal lobes... and contains the circle of Willis[cite: 17].

questionBank.question: Which cistern lies posterior to the chiasmatic cistern and contains the terminal basilar artery and the oculomotor (IIIrd cranial) nerves?
questionBank.explanation: The chiasmatic cistern leads posteriorly to the interpeduncular or intercrural cistern, which contains the terminal basilar artery and its branches and the oculomotor (IIIrd cranial) nerves[cite: 18].

questionBank.question: The ambient cistern surrounds the midbrain and transmits several critical structures. Which cranial nerve travels within it?
questionBank.explanation: The ambient cistern surrounds the midbrain and transmits the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, the basal veins of Rosenthal and the trochlear nerves[cite: 18].

questionBank.question: The quadrigeminal cistern lies adjacent to the superior surface of the cerebellum. Which vascular confluence is located here?

options.label: A
options.text: Confluence of the transverse and superior sagittal sinuses

options.label: B
options.text: Junction of the inferior petrosal sinus and jugular bulb

options.label: C
options.text: Junction of the vein of Galen with the inferior sagittal and straight sinuses

options.label: D
options.text: Confluence of the basal veins of Rosenthal and the internal cerebral veins

questionBank.answer: Junction of the vein of Galen with the inferior sagittal and straight sinuses
questionBank.explanation: The quadrigeminal cistern... is also the location of the venous confluence where the vein of Galen joins the inferior sagittal and straight dural venous sinuses[cite: 18].

questionBank.question: Which cistern contains the anterior communicating artery?
questionBank.explanation: The cistern of the lamina terminalis is superior to the chiasmatic cistern. It contains the anterior communicating artery[cite: 18].

questionBank.question: On T2-weighted MRI images, why do the red nuclei within the midbrain appear hypointense?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to their high iron content

options.label: B
options.text: Due to their high lipid content

questionBank.explanation: The red nuclei are hypointense on T2W images due to their vascularity and the substantia nigra due to their iron content[cite: 19].

questionBank.question: Which two cranial nerves arise in the midbrain?
questionBank.explanation: Cranial nerves arising in the midbrain are the oculomotor (IIIrd) and the trochlear (IVth)[cite: 19].

questionBank.question: The oculomotor (IIIrd) nerve passes between which two arteries immediately after exiting the midbrain?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior cerebral and middle cerebral arteries

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

options.label: C
options.text: Superior cerebellar and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries

options.label: D
options.text: Vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries

questionBank.answer: Posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
questionBank.explanation: The oculomotor (IIIrd) arises from the anterior midbrain... and passes between the superior cerebellar and posterior communicating arteries. Aneurysms arising at the origins of either of these two arteries can cause a IIIrd nerve palsy (Note: Image 1.19 and text describe it traversing adjacent to posterior communicating, but technically passes between posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar in standard anatomy; text states 'passes between the superior cerebellar and posterior communicating arteries')[cite: 19].

questionBank.question: Which unique feature describes the anatomical origin of the trochlear (IVth) cranial nerve?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the only nerve to exit the brainstem through the pontomedullary junction.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the largest of the true cranial nerves.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the only cranial nerve arising from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem.

options.label: D
options.text: It arises laterally from the middle cerebellar peduncle.

questionBank.answer: It is the only cranial nerve arising from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem.
questionBank.explanation: The trochlear (IVth) nerve is the smallest in calibre, has the longest intracranial course and is the only cranial nerve arising from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem[cite: 19].

questionBank.question: Which cranial nerve arises precisely at the junction of the pons and the middle cerebellar peduncle?
questionBank.explanation: The trigeminal (Vth) is the largest of the true cranial nerves and arises at the junction of pons and middle cerebellar peduncle[cite: 20].

questionBank.question: The abducent (VIth) nerve passes into the cavernous sinus through which named bony canal?
questionBank.explanation: The abducent (VIth) has a relatively long intracranial course, passing in an anterolateral direction through Dorello's canal into the cavernous sinus[cite: 20].

questionBank.question: Which four cranial nerves arise from the medulla?
questionBank.explanation: Cranial nerves arising from the medulla are, from above down, the glossopharyngeal (IXth), the vagus (Xth), the spinal accessory (XIth) and the hypoglossal (XIIth)[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: The glossopharyngeal (IXth) and vagus (Xth) cranial nerves arise from a sulcus located where on the medulla?
questionBank.explanation: The glossopharyngeal (IXth) and the vagus (Xth) cranial nerves arise from a sulcus posterolateral to the olive[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: Which cranial nerve arises from the pre-olivary sulcus of the medulla?
questionBank.explanation: The hypoglossal (XIIth) nerve arises from the pre-olivary sulcus[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: Which cerebellar peduncle is the largest and connects the cerebellum to the pons?
questionBank.explanation: There are three cerebellar peduncles... the inferior cerebellar peduncle joins the medulla, the middle cerebellar peduncle (the largest) the pons and the superior, the midbrain[cite: 22].

questionBank.question: Why does the normal cerebellar flocculus appear to enhance more than the rest of the cerebellum on CT following intravenous contrast?

options.label: B
options.text: It contains high concentrations of calcified arachnoid granulations.

options.label: C
options.text: It is in close proximity to the choroid plexus and anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

options.label: D
options.text: It is supplied directly by the highly vascular middle meningeal artery.

questionBank.answer: It is in close proximity to the choroid plexus and anterior inferior cerebellar artery.
questionBank.explanation: The normal flocculus appears to enhance more than the rest of the cerebellum on CT after intravenous contrast because of its proximity to the choroid plexus and anterior inferior cerebellar artery[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: Which structure is the most ventral on the inferior vermian surface and can be identified indenting the fourth ventricle on axial scans?
questionBank.explanation: The nodule is the most ventral structure on the inferior vermian surface and is identified on axial scans indenting the fourth ventricle[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: What are the cortical ridges of the cerebellum called?
questionBank.explanation: The cortical mantle overlies the white matter core as in the cerebral hemispheres but the cerebellar cortical ridges, known as the folia, and the intervening sulci are approximately parallel to one another[cite: 21].

questionBank.question: Which segment of the internal carotid artery runs horizontally through the petrous bone?
questionBank.explanation: The artery enters the cranial cavity through the carotid canal in the petrous bone, running first vertically then horizontally (C2 segment)[cite: 23].

questionBank.question: The cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery is designated as which segment?
questionBank.explanation: C4 is the cavernous segment. The artery turns forwards in the cavernous sinus then upwards to form the clinoid (C5) segment[cite: 23].

questionBank.question: Which branch of the internal carotid artery is the first supraclinoid branch recognizable on normal angiography?
questionBank.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is the first supraclinoid branch of the ICA recognizable on normal angiography. It arises in the subarachnoid space and runs forward through the optic canal[cite: 24].

questionBank.question: The anterior choroidal artery enters the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle through which structure?
questionBank.explanation: The anterior choroidal artery enters into the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle through the choroidal fissure into the choroid plexus[cite: 24].

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the circle of Willis?

options.label: A
options.text: First part of the anterior cerebral arteries (A1)

questionBank.explanation: The participating arteries are the terminal ICAs, the first part of the anterior cerebral arteries (A1 segments), the anterior communicating artery, the posterior communicating arteries, the first parts of the posterior cerebral arteries (P1 segments) and the basilar artery[cite: 25].

questionBank.question: Which artery is the largest of the perforating medial lenticulostriate branches?
questionBank.explanation: Heubner's recurrent artery is the largest of the perforating medial lenticulostriate branches which course posterosuperiorly[cite: 26].

questionBank.question: The M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery runs laterally to which anatomical landmark?

options.label: A
options.text: Horizontal limb of the Sylvian fissure

questionBank.answer: Horizontal limb of the Sylvian fissure
questionBank.explanation: Its proximal portion, the M1 segment, runs laterally to the horizontal limb of the Sylvian fissure between the frontal and temporal lobes[cite: 26].

questionBank.question: Which dural venous sinus is located at the junction of the falx and the tentorium?
questionBank.explanation: The straight sinus lies at the junction of the falx and the tentorium and the torcular is where the straight, transverse and superior sagittal sinuses meet[cite: 27].

questionBank.question: The vein of Galen joins which two sinuses at the venous confluence within the quadrigeminal plate cistern?
questionBank.explanation: The vein of Galen (the great cerebral vein) joins the inferior sagittal and straight sinuses at the venous confluence within the quadrigeminal plate system (venous confluence 2)[cite: 27].

questionBank.question: Which cranial nerve lies free within the cavernous sinus applied to the lateral wall of the internal carotid artery?
questionBank.explanation: The abducent nerve lies free within the sinus applied to the lateral wall of the artery[cite: 29].

questionBank.question: Which anastomotic vein connects the superficial middle cerebral vein with the superior sagittal sinus?
questionBank.explanation: The anastomostic veins of Trolard, superiorly, and Labbe, inferiorly, connect the superficial middle cerebral vein with superior sagittal and transverse sinuses, respectively[cite: 29].

questionBank.question: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) usually arises from which artery?
questionBank.explanation: PICA arises from the vertebral artery as its largest and most distal branch[cite: 31].

questionBank.question: The basilar artery is formed by the confluence of the vertebral arteries at which anatomical location?
questionBank.explanation: The basilar artery forms from the confluence of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction[cite: 31].

questionBank.question: The P2 (ambient) segment of the posterior cerebral artery may be compressed against which structure during raised intracranial pressure, potentially causing occipital lobe infarction?
questionBank.explanation: The P2 segment may be compressed against the tentorial edge when there is uncal pressure on the midbrain in the presence of raised intracranial pressure. Infarction of the occipital lobe is thus a recognized consequence[cite: 32].

questionBank.question: What is the most dorsal nucleus of the thalamus called?
questionBank.explanation: The thalamus is the largest structure in the diencephalon and is made up of a number of functionally important nuclei. The most dorsal nucleus is called the pulvinar[cite: 32].

questionBank.question: The pituitary 'bright spot' seen on T1-weighted MRI is due to the presence of vasopressin/oxytocin in which part of the gland?
questionBank.explanation: The neurohypophysis often has a conspicuous appearance on T1W images due to the presence of vasopressin/oxytocin - the so-called pituitary 'bright spot'[cite: 33].

questionBank.question: Which basal ganglia structure has a head that indents the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle and a tail that lies superior to the temporal horn?
questionBank.explanation: The head of the caudate nucleus indents the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Its body curves upwards... to its thinnest part, the tail, which comes to lie immediately superior to the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle[cite: 34, 36].

questionBank.question: Damage to the subthalamic nucleus results in which neurological condition?
questionBank.explanation: Damage to this nucleus results in contralateral hemiballismus - uncontrolled jerks of the limbs[cite: 36].

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the outer arch of the limbic lobe?
questionBank.explanation: Outer arch: parahippocampal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, subcallosal gyrus. Middle arch: hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus, indusium griseum, paraterminal gyrus[cite: 36].

questionBank.question: The fimbria of the hippocampal formation continues as which structure?
questionBank.explanation: The fimbria of the hippocampal formation continues as the crus of the fornix, a fibre bundle that sweeps backwards, upwards and medially around the posterior aspect of the thalamus[cite: 37].

questionBank.question: In the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), which body part takes up the largest area of cortical representation?
questionBank.explanation: Upper limb takes up the largest area of cortical representation (situated between lower limb and head/face)[cite: 39].

questionBank.question: Which two gyri in the parietal lobe are involved in visuospatial processing, particularly in the non-dominant hemisphere?
questionBank.explanation: The parietal lobe also contains two further important gyri: the supramarginal and angular gyri, which are involved in visuospatial processing (especially in the non-dominant hemisphere)[cite: 39].

questionBank.question: Wernicke's area, involved with the receptive aspects of speech, is situated where?

options.label: A
options.text: Pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus

options.label: C
options.text: Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus

questionBank.answer: Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus
questionBank.explanation: The temporal lobe also contains Wernicke's area (in the dominant hemisphere), which is involved with the receptive aspects of speech and is situated in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, inferior to the angular gyrus[cite: 39].

questionBank.question: The medial surface of the occipital lobe is made up of the cuneus above and which structure below?
questionBank.explanation: The medial surface of the occipital lobe is made up of the cuneus (above) and the lingula (below)[cite: 40].

questionBank.question: The posterior limb of the internal capsule is supplied by which artery?
questionBank.explanation: The blood vessels supplying the internal capsule are... posterior limb - anterior choroidal artery (arises from the internal carotid artery)[cite: 43].

questionBank.question: The anterior commissure links the olfactory tracts and structures within the anterior temporal lobes. Where is it embedded?

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior wall of the third ventricle (lamina terminalis)

questionBank.answer: Anterior wall of the third ventricle (lamina terminalis)
questionBank.explanation: It lies in front of the columns of the fornices, embedded in the anterior wall of the third ventricle (the lamina terminalis)[cite: 43].

questionBank.question: The cavum septi pellucidi persists into adulthood in approximately what percentage of people?
questionBank.explanation: It persists into adulthood in about 10% of people[cite: 44].

questionBank.question: Which recess is located directly behind the infundibulum of the pituitary gland in the third ventricle?
questionBank.explanation: ...and the more inferior lies behind the infundibulum of the pituitary gland (the infundibular recess)[cite: 44].

questionBank.question: The olfactory tract divides into medial and lateral tracts at which anatomical point?
questionBank.explanation: It divides into medial and lateral tracts at the olfactory trigone, a point in the basal forebrain just in front of the anterior perforated substance[cite: 38].

questionBank.question: The fibers of the splenium of the corpus callosum curve backward into the occipital lobes to form which structure?
questionBank.explanation: Similarly, the fibres of the splenium curve backward into the occipital lobes, as forceps major[cite: 43].

questionBank.question: Which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The falx cerebri is a dural fold between the cerebral hemispheres.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The falx cerebri is a dural fold between the cerebral hemispheres.

questionBank.question: Which option identifies the correct structure? Which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The falx cerebri is a dural fold between the cerebral hemispheres.

questionBank.question: Choose the best anatomical answer: Which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The falx cerebri is a dural fold between the cerebral hemispheres.

questionBank.question: For an imaging review, which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The falx cerebri is a dural fold between the cerebral hemispheres.

questionBank.question: Which ventricle lies between the thalami?
questionBank.explanation: The third ventricle is the midline cavity between the thalami.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which ventricle lies between the thalami?
questionBank.explanation: The third ventricle is the midline cavity between the thalami.

questionBank.question: Which option identifies the correct structure? Which ventricle lies between the thalami?

questionBank.question: Which structure connects the third and fourth ventricles?
questionBank.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct traverses the midbrain and links the third and fourth ventricles.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which structure connects the third and fourth ventricles?
questionBank.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct traverses the midbrain and links the third and fourth ventricles.

questionBank.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct traverses the midbrain and links the third and fourth ventricles.

questionBank.question: Which artery is a major source of the anterior cerebral circulation?
questionBank.explanation: The internal carotid arteries supply most of the anterior cerebral circulation.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which artery is a major source of the anterior cerebral circulation?
questionBank.explanation: The internal carotid arteries supply most of the anterior cerebral circulation.

questionBank.question: Which option identifies the correct structure? Which artery is a major source of the anterior cerebral circulation?
questionBank.explanation: The internal carotid arteries supply most of the anterior cerebral circulation.

questionBank.explanation: The internal carotid arteries supply most of the anterior cerebral circulation.

questionBank.question: Which dural venous sinus runs along the attached superior margin of the falx?
questionBank.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which dural venous sinus runs along the attached superior margin of the falx?
questionBank.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri.

questionBank.question: Which option identifies the correct structure? Which dural venous sinus runs along the attached superior margin of the falx?
questionBank.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri.

questionBank.question: For an imaging review, which dural venous sinus runs along the attached superior margin of the falx?
questionBank.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri.

questionBank.question: Which structure forms the major commissural connection between the cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The corpus callosum is the principal commissural fibre bundle between hemispheres.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which structure forms the major commissural connection between the cerebral hemispheres?
questionBank.explanation: The corpus callosum is the principal commissural fibre bundle between hemispheres.

questionBank.explanation: The corpus callosum is the principal commissural fibre bundle between hemispheres.

questionBank.explanation: Non-contrast CT is fast and sensitive to acute blood.

questionBank.question: Which lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
questionBank.explanation: The primary visual cortex lies around the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe.

questionBank.question: In normal anatomy, which lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
questionBank.explanation: The primary visual cortex lies around the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe.

questionBank.question: Which of the following describes the relationship of the posterior part of the optic chiasm to the third ventricle?

options.label: A
options.text: It forms the floor of the third ventricle.

options.label: B
options.text: It contributes to the anterior wall of the third ventricle.

options.label: C
options.text: It forms the roof of the third ventricle.

options.label: D
options.text: It contributes to the posterior wall of the third ventricle.

questionBank.answer: It contributes to the anterior wall of the third ventricle.
questionBank.explanation: The posterior part of the chiasm contributes to the anterior wall of the third ventricle, with the optic recess above and the infundibular recess below[cite: 54].

questionBank.question: The optic tracts run posterolaterally and merge with brain substance to terminate at which structure on the posterior aspect of the thalamus?
questionBank.explanation: They merge with brain substance as they course posteriorly to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), an elevated region of grey matter on the posterior aspect of the thalamus, lateral to the pulvinar[cite: 54].

questionBank.question: Which visual field fibres form Meyer's loop by sweeping inferiorly around the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle?
questionBank.explanation: The superior visual field fibres sweep inferiorly around the temporal horn, forming Meyer's loop[cite: 54].

questionBank.question: The primary visual cortex is located along the superior and inferior margins of which specific fissure?
questionBank.explanation: The visual cortex is located along the superior and inferior margins of the calcarine fissure on the medial aspect of the occipital lobe[cite: 54].

questionBank.question: Where is the inferior contralateral visual field represented in the visual cortex?

options.label: A
options.text: On the inferior aspect of the calcarine fissure

options.label: B
options.text: On the superior aspect of the calcarine fissure

questionBank.answer: On the superior aspect of the calcarine fissure
questionBank.explanation: The inferior contralateral visual field lies on the superior aspect of the fissure, the superior contralateral visual field on its inferior aspect[cite: 54].

questionBank.question: What term describes the disproportionate extent of cortex occupied by the representation of the central visual field and fovea?
questionBank.explanation: The two occupy a disproportionate extent of cortex compared to the peripheral field ('cortical magnification')[cite: 55].

questionBank.question: A lesion located at the optic chiasm typically results in which specific visual field defect?
questionBank.explanation: A lesion at the optic chiasm results in bitemporal hemianopia[cite: 55].

questionBank.question: A lesion affecting the optic radiation within the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) will result in which visual field defect?
questionBank.explanation: A lesion of the optic radiation, temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) results in homonymous superior quadrantopia[cite: 55].

questionBank.question: Why is the macula typically spared in a case of posterior cerebral artery occlusion affecting the occipital lobe?

options.label: A
options.text: The macula is represented in the anterior visual cortex, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

options.label: B
options.text: The macula is represented in the posterior visual cortex, which receives additional supply from middle cerebral artery branches.

options.label: C
options.text: The macular fibres travel in the medial optic tract, avoiding the occlusion.

options.label: D
options.text: The macular fibres bypass the visual cortex and terminate in the superior colliculus.

questionBank.answer: The macula is represented in the posterior visual cortex, which receives additional supply from middle cerebral artery branches.
questionBank.explanation: A calcarine cortex lesion (e.g. posterior cerebral artery occlusion) results in homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing because the macula is represented in the posterior visual cortex, with supply from middle cerebral artery branches[cite: 55].

questionBank.answer: It is a bony septum of variable thickness forming part of the petrosquamosal suture that passes through the mastoid antrum.
questionBank.explanation: This is a bony septum of variable thickness and is part of the petrosquamosal suture. It is a surgical landmark and passes through the antrum, where it can be confused with the medial wall of the antrum at surgery[cite: 60].

questionBank.question: The cochleariform process serves as a landmark for the tendon of which muscle as it turns laterally to attach to the neck of the malleus?
questionBank.explanation: The cochleariform process is a depression in the anterior aspect of the medial wall marking the point where the tensor tympani muscle turns laterally to attach to the neck of the malleus[cite: 57, 58].

questionBank.question: What is the central bony axis of the cochlea from which the spiral lamina projects?
questionBank.explanation: The modiolus is the central axis from which a thin bony plate (the spiral lamina) projects and attaches to the outer cochlea wall[cite: 60].

questionBank.question: Which narrow channel containing perilymph connects the scala tympani of the basal turn directly with the subarachnoid space?
questionBank.explanation: The cochlear aqueduct... is a narrow channel containing perilymph that connects the scala tympani of the basal turn with the subarachnoid space[cite: 61].

questionBank.question: Within the vestibule of the inner ear, which structure is positioned anteriorly?
questionBank.explanation: The vestibule... contains the saccule (anterior) and the utricle (posterior) which cannot yet be clearly differentiated on routine imaging[cite: 61].

questionBank.question: The bony covering of which semicircular canal forms the arcuate eminence on the superior surface of the petrous bone?
questionBank.explanation: The bony covering of the superior semicircular canal forms the arcuate eminence, a ridge on the superior surface of the petrous bone that can be seen also on skull radiographs[cite: 62].

questionBank.question: The nerve of the posterior semicircular canal initially passes through a separate canal before joining the inferior vestibular nerve. What is this canal called?
questionBank.explanation: Commonly the nerve of the PSCC passes initially in a separate canal, the singular canal, which is clearly visible on HRCT prior to joining the inferior vestibular nerve in the IAC[cite: 62].

questionBank.question: At the porus acousticus (the medial opening of the internal auditory canal), what is the normal arrangement of the cranial nerves?

options.label: A
options.text: The facial nerve is larger and posterior to the vestibulocochlear nerve

options.label: B
options.text: The vestibulocochlear nerve is larger and posterior to the facial nerve

options.label: C
options.text: The cochlear nerve is superior to the facial nerve

options.label: D
options.text: The vestibulocochlear nerve is superior to the facial nerve

questionBank.answer: The vestibulocochlear nerve is larger and posterior to the facial nerve
questionBank.explanation: At the porus acousticus, the medial opening of the IAC, there are usually only two distinct nerves visible... the larger and more posterior vestibulocochlear (VIIIth cranial) nerve and the smaller, more anterior facial nerve[cite: 63].

questionBank.question: Which bony structure horizontally divides the fundus (lateral portion) of the internal auditory canal into halves?
questionBank.explanation: The fundus is divided into halves by the horizontal crista falciformis, a bony bar of variable size that is clearly seen on HRCT[cite: 64].

questionBank.question: At the fundus of the internal auditory canal, in which quadrant does the cochlear nerve lie?
questionBank.explanation: At the fundus... the vestibulocochlear (VIIIth cranial) nerve has divided into a separate cochlear nerve anterorinferiorly seen entering the modiolus and the superior and inferior vestibular nerves in the posterosuperior and posteroinferior quadrants, respectively[cite: 63].

questionBank.question: Which segment of the intratemporal facial nerve is the shortest and narrowest, extending anterolaterally from the IAC to the geniculate ganglion?
questionBank.explanation: The first (labyrinthine) segment of the facial nerve is the narrowest and shortest segment and extends anterolaterally from the IAC superior to the cochlea, terminating at the geniculate ganglion[cite: 64].

questionBank.question: The greater superficial petrosal nerve arises from the geniculate ganglion to supply secretomotor fibres to which structure?
questionBank.explanation: The most proximal branch of the facial nerve is the greater superficial petrosal nerve, which extends anteriorly from the geniculate ganglion in a small groove to supply secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland and receive taste fibres from the hard palate[cite: 64, 65].

questionBank.question: On coronal HRCT, the classic 'snakes eyes' appearance is produced by the cross-sections of which two segments of the facial nerve?

options.label: B
options.text: Distal labyrinthine and proximal tympanic segments

options.label: D
options.text: Greater superficial petrosal and chorda tympani nerves

questionBank.answer: Distal labyrinthine and proximal tympanic segments
questionBank.explanation: The classic 'snakes eyes' appearance of the facial nerve is seen on coronal scans... when it passes through both the distal labyrinthine and proximal tympanic segments on the same image just posterior to the geniculate ganglion[cite: 65].

questionBank.question: The chorda tympani nerve branches off the mastoid segment of the facial nerve to carry afferent taste fibres from which region?
questionBank.explanation: The chorda tympani originates just above the stylomastoid foramen... It carries afferent taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and efferent secretomotor fibres to sublingual, submandibular and minor salivary glands[cite: 65].

questionBank.question: The smaller anterior part of the jugular foramen is called the pars nervosa. Which cranial nerve is transmitted through this compartment?
questionBank.explanation: The jugular foramen... is divided into two parts, a smaller anterior pars nervosa, which despite its name contains only the glossopharyngeal (IXth cranial) nerve, and Jacobsen's nerve... and drains the inferior petrosal sinus[cite: 65].

questionBank.question: In cross-sectional imaging, how is a 'high-riding' jugular bulb defined anatomically?

options.label: A
options.text: The superior aspect of the bulb extends above the floor of the internal auditory canal (IAC)

options.label: B
options.text: The bulb compresses the geniculate ganglion

options.label: C
options.text: The bulb extends above the tegmen tympani

options.label: D
options.text: The bulb protrudes into the external auditory canal

questionBank.answer: The superior aspect of the bulb extends above the floor of the internal auditory canal (IAC)
questionBank.explanation: A high-riding jugular bulb is defined when the superior aspect of the bulb extends above the floor of the internal auditory canal (IAC)[cite: 65].

questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: the external auditory canal (EAC) is structurally divided into cartilaginous and bony segments. What is the correct anatomical proportion?

options.label: A
options.text: The lateral one-third is bony and the medial two-thirds cartilaginous

options.label: B
options.text: The lateral one-third is cartilaginous and the medial two-thirds bony

options.label: C
options.text: The lateral two-thirds is cartilaginous and the medial one-third bony

options.label: D
options.text: The lateral one-half is cartilaginous and the medial one-half bony

questionBank.answer: The lateral one-third is cartilaginous and the medial two-thirds bony
questionBank.explanation: The S-shaped EAC extends from the external auditory meatus (EAM) to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous and the medial two-thirds bony[cite: 57].

questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. What is the anterior anatomical relation of the external auditory canal?

options.label: B
options.text: The mandibular fossa containing the mandibular condyle

questionBank.answer: The mandibular fossa containing the mandibular condyle
questionBank.explanation: The anatomical relations of the EAC are... anteriorly: the mandibular fossa containing the mandibular condyle and temporomandibular joint[cite: 57].

questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, the lymphatic drainage from the external auditory canal is primarily directed to which nodal group?
questionBank.explanation: The nodal drainage from the EAC is to the intraparotid group[cite: 57].

questionBank.question: The tympanic membrane is attached superiorly to which bony structure?
questionBank.explanation: The TM is usually visible in the coronal plane as a thin line on HRCT and is attached superiorly to the scutum (shield)... and peripherally to a bony annulus[cite: 57].

questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, which structure on the medial wall of the middle ear overlies the basal turn of the cochlea?
questionBank.explanation: The cochlear promontory overlies the basal turn of the cochlea, with the oval window superior and the round window posteroinferior to it[cite: 57].

questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: on the posterior wall of the middle ear cavity, the pyramidal eminence separates the facial recess from which other structure?
questionBank.explanation: The pyramidal eminence separates the sinus tympani medially from the facial recess laterally[cite: 58].

questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. Which muscle extends from the pyramidal eminence to attach to the neck of the stapes?
questionBank.explanation: The stapedius muscle extends from the pyramidal eminence to attach to the neck of the stapes[cite: 58].

questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, the thin bony plate covering the roof of the tympanic cavity, separating it from the middle cranial fossa, is called the:
questionBank.explanation: The tegmen is the thin bony plate covering the roof of the tympanic cavity separating it from the middle cranial fossa[cite: 58].

questionBank.question: An aberrant internal carotid artery in the middle ear presents as a retrotympanic vascular mass over the cochlear promontory. This develops as a collateral circulation due to the failure of which structure to develop?

options.label: D
options.text: The first embryonic segment of the internal carotid artery

questionBank.answer: The first embryonic segment of the internal carotid artery
questionBank.explanation: This is a collateral circulation secondary to failure of development of the first embryonic segment of the ICA. The collateral route is via the inferior tympanic artery... by coursing over the cochlear promontory and is seen as a retrotympanic vascular mass[cite: 58, 59].

questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, on axial HRCT imaging, the 'ice cream on a cone' appearance represents the articulation between which two structures?

options.label: A
options.text: Long process of the incus and the stapes crura

options.label: B
options.text: Handle of the malleus and the tympanic membrane

options.label: C
options.text: Head of the malleus and body of the incus

options.label: D
options.text: Lenticular process of the incus and head of the stapes

questionBank.answer: Head of the malleus and body of the incus
questionBank.explanation: On axial images the malleoincudal joint resembles an ice cream (head of malleus) sitting on a cone (body of incus)[cite: 59].

questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: which two parts of the incus meet at an angle of approximately 90 degrees to form a 'hockey stick' appearance on coronal HRCT?
questionBank.explanation: The long and lenticular processes meet at an angle of approximately 90°. This 'hockey stick' appearance is best demonstrated in the coronal plane[cite: 59].

questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. The space located between the anterior and posterior crura of the stapes is known as the:
questionBank.explanation: The space between the stapes crura is called the obturator foramen[cite: 59].

questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, prussak's space is a clinically significant anatomical region because it is the most common site of origin for which pathology?
questionBank.explanation: Prussak's space is the most common site of origin for acquired cholesteatoma and is located between the lateral mallear ligament superiorly, the lateral (short) process of the malleus inferiorly, the pars flaccida of the TM laterally and the neck of the malleus medially[cite: 59].

questionBank.question: Which of the following describes Koerner's septum?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the bony covering of the superior semicircular canal.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a thin cartilaginous plate separating the external auditory canal from the middle ear.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a bony septum of variable thickness forming part of the petrosquamosal suture that passes through the mastoid antrum.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a fibrous band securing the malleus to the tegmen tympani.

questionBank.answer: It is a bony septum of variable thickness forming part of the petrosquamosal suture that passes through the mastoid antrum.
questionBank.explanation: This is a bony septum of variable thickness and is part of the petrosquamosal suture. It is a surgical landmark and passes through the antrum, where it can be confused with the medial wall of the antrum at surgery[cite: 60].

questionBank.question: The superficial (investing) layer of the deep cervical fascia envelops the parotid and masticator spaces, as well as which two muscles?
questionBank.explanation: The superficial layer invests all the deep structures apart from the platysma and superficial nodes and sends slips that envelop the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and the parotid and masticator spaces[cite: 66].

questionBank.question: Which specific anatomical space in the suprahyoid neck is described as an inverted pyramid extending from the skull base to its apex at the hyoid bone?
questionBank.explanation: The PPS is located centrally within the suprahyoid neck and is an inverted pyramid extending from the skull base to its apex at the hyoid bone[cite: 67].

questionBank.question: Which anatomical structure separates the superficial and deep 'lobes' (components) of the parotid gland?
questionBank.explanation: The gland is encapsulated by the superficial layer of cervical fascia... and is described as having superficial and deep 'lobes' separated by the facial nerve[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) turns 90 degrees to pierce which muscle before opening into the oral cavity at the level of the second upper molar?
questionBank.explanation: The parotid duct is around 7 cm long and emerges from the anterior parotid superficial to the masseter muscle, then turns 90° to pierce the buccinator muscle to open into the oral cavity at the level of the second upper molar[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: The superficial and deep parts of the submandibular gland connect around the posterior border of which muscle?
questionBank.explanation: The submandibular gland has superficial and deep parts that connect around the posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: The submandibular duct opens into the oral cavity at which specific location?

options.label: A
options.text: At the level of the second upper molar

options.label: B
options.text: At the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth

questionBank.answer: At the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth
questionBank.explanation: It then passes anteriorly between the mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles... before opening at the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: Which paired muscle lies immediately medial to the distal submandibular duct, separating it from the midline?
questionBank.explanation: It lies on the sublingual groove of the mandible, with the distal submandibular duct separating it from the more medial genioglossus muscle[cite: 70].

questionBank.question: What structure forms the anterior limit of the nasopharynx?
questionBank.explanation: The anterior limit of the nasopharynx is the nasal choanae; the sloping roof is formed by the central skull base[cite: 71].

questionBank.question: The lateral pharyngeal recess, located just posterior to the eustachian tube orifice, is the most common site of origin for nasopharyngeal carcinomas. What is another name for this recess?
questionBank.explanation: The lateral wall is composed of the cartilaginous Eustachian tube... with the eustachian tube orifice seen just anterior and the lateral pharyngeal recess or fossa of Rosenmuller just posterior to it. The fossa of Rosenmuller is... the commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinomas[cite: 71, 72].

questionBank.question: The boundary dividing the nasopharynx from the oropharynx is defined by which structure(s)?

options.label: B
options.text: The hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level

questionBank.answer: The hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level
questionBank.explanation: The division between the nasopharynx and oropharynx is the hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level[cite: 71].

questionBank.question: The anterior tonsillar pillar is a mucosal fold that overlies which specific muscle?
questionBank.explanation: The anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars are both mucosal folds overlying muscles (palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus, respectively) that merge superiorly into the soft palate[cite: 73].

questionBank.question: A pharyngeal pouch may form through a potential weak area located between which two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle?
questionBank.explanation: The inferior constrictor muscle... consists of two parts, the more superior obliquely oriented thyropharyngeus and the horizontal more inferior cricopharyngeus; between the two is a potential weak area through which a pharyngeal pouch may form[cite: 73].

questionBank.question: What structure forms the anteromedial boundary of the pyriform sinus, separating it from the larynx?
questionBank.explanation: The boundaries of the pyriform sinus are laterally the posterior thyroid lamina, posteriorly the lateral aspect of the posterior pharyngeal wall and anteromedially the aryepiglottic fold, which separates it from the larynx[cite: 73].

questionBank.question: The true vocal cords attach posteriorly to the anterior vocal processes of which laryngeal cartilages?
questionBank.explanation: The arytenoid cartilages are pyramidal in shape, sit on top of the cricoid lamina and consist of anterior vocal processes to which the posterior vocal cord is attached[cite: 75].

questionBank.question: The false cords (vestibular folds) are formed by the mucosal surface of which anatomical structures?
questionBank.explanation: The inferior margin of the aryepiglottic fold is free and the mucosal surface of the aryepiglottic folds forms the false cords[cite: 75].

questionBank.question: The retropharyngeal space provides a potential route for infection to spread to the mediastinum. It extends from the skull base down to which vertebral level?
questionBank.explanation: The retropharyngeal space is a potential space between the middle and deep layers of cervical fascia, extending from the skull base to T4[cite: 75].

questionBank.question: Which muscle of mastication inserts specifically onto the medial mandibular condyle?
questionBank.explanation: The muscles of mastication insert onto the mandible: the lateral pterygoid onto the medial mandibular condyle[cite: 75].

questionBank.question: The masticator space contains the muscles of mastication and which major nerve?

options.label: A
options.text: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve

questionBank.answer: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
questionBank.explanation: The mandible and surrounding muscles of mastication are invested by the superficial layer of deep cervical fascia to form the masticator space, which contains the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve[cite: 75].

questionBank.question: The temporomandibular joint is divided into two separate compartments by a fibrous disc. In which compartment does translational movement occur?

options.label: A
options.text: Between the condyle and the inferior aspect of the disc

options.label: B
options.text: Between the glenoid fossa and the superior surface of the disc

options.label: D
options.text: Between the articular eminence and the anterior band

questionBank.answer: Between the glenoid fossa and the superior surface of the disc

questionBank.question: At approximately which vertebral level does the common carotid artery (CCA) typically bifurcate into the internal and external carotid arteries?
questionBank.explanation: The bifurcation of the CCA into internal and external branches (ICA and ECA) occurs at the level of C4 (hyoid bone)[cite: 78].

questionBank.question: The ostiomeatal unit (OMU) is responsible for draining which three paranasal sinuses?

options.text: Frontal, posterior ethmoidal, and sphenoid sinuses

options.label: B
options.text: Frontal, anterior ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses

options.label: C
options.text: Maxillary, sphenoid, and posterior ethmoidal sinuses

options.text: Anterior ethmoidal, posterior ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses

questionBank.answer: Frontal, anterior ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses
questionBank.explanation: The ostiomeatal unit (OMU) drains the frontal, anterior ethmoidal and maxillary sinuses[cite: 78].

questionBank.question: Which specific air cell is the most anterior of the ethmoidal air cells and can displace the frontal recess posteriorly if it becomes enlarged?
questionBank.explanation: The agger nasi air cell (ANC) is the most anterior of the ethmoidal air cells and may vary in size. If large it can displace the frontal recess posteriorly and narrow the ostium[cite: 79].

questionBank.question: Infraorbital air cells that extend along the orbital floor and may compromise the outflow of the maxillary sinus are also known by what name?
questionBank.explanation: Infraorbital (Haller) air cells are centred inferior to the ethmoidal bulla, extend along the orbital floor and may compromise the outflow[cite: 80].

questionBank.question: During endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery, several critical structures projecting into the sphenoid sinus are at risk because they may have a dehiscent bony covering. Which of the following is NOT one of these structures?
questionBank.explanation: There are also a number of important structures, closely related to the sphenoid sinus, which may project into the sinus and which may have a dehiscent bony covering. These are the optic nerve, the maxillary nerve, the vidian canal and the intracavernous segment of the internal carotid artery[cite: 80].

questionBank.question: The posterior portion of the nasal septum is formed by the vomer and which other bony structure?
questionBank.explanation: The nasal septum comprises the septal cartilage anteriorly and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer posteriorly[cite: 80].

questionBank.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates medially with the nasal cavity via which structure?
questionBank.explanation: It is the 'junction box' of the deep neck as it communicates with multiple anatomical sites: medially, the nasal cavity via the sphenopalatine foramen[cite: 81].

questionBank.question: Which is the largest of the paired extrinsic muscles of the tongue, fanning out posteriorly from the anterior mandible?
questionBank.explanation: The largest of these is the genioglossus, which arises anteriorly from the genial tubercle on the lingual surface of the anterior mandible and fans out posteriorly into the tongue[cite: 81].

questionBank.question: During embryonic development, the thyroid gland descends into the neck via the thyroglossal duct from which specific structure in the midline of the tongue base?
questionBank.explanation: During development the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum in the midline of the tongue base on the end of the thyroglossal duct[cite: 82].

questionBank.question: The jugulodigastric node is the most frequently involved node in squamous cell carcinomas of the tonsil. In which cervical nodal level is it located?
questionBank.explanation: The most important node of this chain is the jugulodigastric node in the upper deep cervical region as it is the most frequently involved node in squamous cell carcinomas of the tonsil, lateral tongue base and supraglottic larynx[cite: 83]. questionBank.question: The superficial (investing) layer of the deep cervical fascia envelops the parotid and masticator spaces, as well as which two muscles?
questionBank.explanation: The superficial layer invests all the deep structures apart from the platysma and superficial nodes and sends slips that envelop the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and the parotid and masticator spaces[cite: 66].

questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, which specific anatomical space in the suprahyoid neck is described as an inverted pyramid extending from the skull base to its apex at the hyoid bone?
questionBank.explanation: The PPS is located centrally within the suprahyoid neck and is an inverted pyramid extending from the skull base to its apex at the hyoid bone[cite: 67].

questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: which anatomical structure separates the superficial and deep 'lobes' (components) of the parotid gland?
questionBank.explanation: The gland is encapsulated by the superficial layer of cervical fascia... and is described as having superficial and deep 'lobes' separated by the facial nerve[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) turns 90 degrees to pierce which muscle before opening into the oral cavity at the level of the second upper molar?
questionBank.explanation: The parotid duct is around 7 cm long and emerges from the anterior parotid superficial to the masseter muscle, then turns 90° to pierce the buccinator muscle to open into the oral cavity at the level of the second upper molar[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, the superficial and deep parts of the submandibular gland connect around the posterior border of which muscle?
questionBank.explanation: The submandibular gland has superficial and deep parts that connect around the posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: The submandibular duct opens into the oral cavity at which specific location?

options.label: B
options.text: At the level of the second upper molar

options.label: C
options.text: At the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth

questionBank.answer: At the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth
questionBank.explanation: It then passes anteriorly between the mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles... before opening at the sublingual papilla in the anterior floor of mouth[cite: 68].

questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, which paired muscle lies immediately medial to the distal submandibular duct, separating it from the midline?
questionBank.explanation: It lies on the sublingual groove of the mandible, with the distal submandibular duct separating it from the more medial genioglossus muscle[cite: 70].

questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: what structure forms the anterior limit of the nasopharynx?
questionBank.explanation: The anterior limit of the nasopharynx is the nasal choanae; the sloping roof is formed by the central skull base[cite: 71].

questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. The lateral pharyngeal recess, located just posterior to the eustachian tube orifice, is the most common site of origin for nasopharyngeal carcinomas. What is another name for this recess?
questionBank.explanation: The lateral wall is composed of the cartilaginous Eustachian tube... with the eustachian tube orifice seen just anterior and the lateral pharyngeal recess or fossa of Rosenmuller just posterior to it. The fossa of Rosenmuller is... the commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinomas[cite: 71, 72].

questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, the boundary dividing the nasopharynx from the oropharynx is defined by which structure(s)?

options.label: A
options.text: The hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level

questionBank.answer: The hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level
questionBank.explanation: The division between the nasopharynx and oropharynx is the hard and soft palate at approximately the C1/2 level[cite: 71].

questionBank.question: The anterior tonsillar pillar is a mucosal fold that overlies which specific muscle?
questionBank.explanation: The anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars are both mucosal folds overlying muscles (palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus, respectively) that merge superiorly into the soft palate[cite: 73].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: A lumbosacral transitional vertebra (LSTV), often termed 'lumbarization' or 'sacralization', occurs in approximately what percentage of the population?
questionBank.explanation: ...variation in the numbering of the last lumbar vertebra occurs with lumbosacral transitional junctions, occurring in ~16% of the population and also being termed 'lumbarization' or 'sacralization'[cite: 85].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In a normal adult, what is the standard range for the cervical lordosis curvature?
questionBank.explanation: Four curvatures are seen in the sagittal plane in adults... cervical lordosis; from C1 to T2, ranging from 30 to 40°[cite: 85].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The atlas (C1) ring is formed by an anterior arch and two neural arches. By what age do the neural arches typically fuse with the anterior arch?
questionBank.explanation: The neural arches fuse by age 3 years to form the posterior arch and fuse with the anterior arch by age 7 years[cite: 86].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In adults, the normal anterior atlanto-dens interval should be less than what measurement?
questionBank.explanation: The normal anterior atlanto-dens interval is <5 mm in children and <3 mm in adults[cite: 87].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In the cervical spine, uncinate processes point superiorly from the posterolateral aspects of the superior end-plate to articulate with the vertebra above. What are these joints called?
questionBank.explanation: Two uncinate processes point superiorly from the posterolateral aspects of the superior end-plate to articulate with the inferior end-plate of the vertebra above, forming the neurocentral joints (of Luschka)[cite: 87].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The posterior boundary of the bony spinal canal is represented on lateral radiographs by which line?

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In the lumbar region, the transverse dimension of the spinal canal is represented radiographically by which measurement?
questionBank.explanation: In the lumbar region, the transverse canal dimension, as represented by the interpediculate distance, should progressively increase from L1 to L5[cite: 88].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The lateral masses of the sacrum are flat and are anatomically termed the:
questionBank.explanation: The S1 body protrudes anteriorly as the sacral promontory, while the lateral masses are flat and are termed the sacral alae[cite: 89].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: From C2 to C6, the foramen transversarium transmits a plexus of sympathetic nerves, the vertebral vein, and which artery?
questionBank.explanation: Each transverse process possesses a foramen transversarium, which from C2-C6 transmits the vertebral artery and vein, as well as a plexus of sympathetic nerves[cite: 90].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The facet (zygoapophyseal) joints are innervated by which specific nerve branch?

questionBank.answer: Medial branch of the dorsal ramus
questionBank.explanation: The facet joints are innervated by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of the mixed spinal nerve[cite: 92].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: What normal anatomical variant describes the asymmetry in the sagittal orientation of the facet joints at the same level, occurring most commonly at L4/L5 and L5/S1?
questionBank.explanation: Facet tropism is a normal variant, occurring most commonly at L4/L5 and L5/S1, referring to asymmetry in the sagittal orientation of the facet joints at the same level[cite: 90].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In adults, why does the vertebral body marrow appear hyperintense relative to the intervertebral disc on T1-weighted MRI?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to a high proportion of red (haemopoietic) marrow

options.label: B
options.text: Due to a high proportion of yellow (fatty) marrow

options.label: C
options.text: Due to increased vascularity in the subchondral bone

options.label: D
options.text: Due to calcification of the trabeculae

questionBank.answer: Due to a high proportion of yellow (fatty) marrow
questionBank.explanation: In adults, the high proportion of yellow marrow results in the marrow appearing hyperintense to the IVD, particularly in the lumbar region[cite: 92].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: At approximately what age does the intervertebral disc become avascular, relying on diffusion through the end-plates for nutrition?
questionBank.explanation: The IVD is avascular by age ~25-30 years, the disc receiving nutrition by diffusion through the end-plates[cite: 93].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The nucleus pulposus appears hyperintense on T2-weighted MRI primarily due to its high content of what substance?
questionBank.explanation: The NP consists of a gel-like substance with ~90% of its content being water, rendering it hyperintense on T2W images[cite: 93].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, the posterior boundary of the bony spinal canal is represented on lateral radiographs by which line?
questionBank.explanation: The bony spinal canal has the following borders: ...posterior, the base of the spinous process, which is represented on lateral radiographs by the spinolaminar line[cite: 88].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: in the lumbar region, the transverse dimension of the spinal canal is represented radiographically by which measurement?
questionBank.explanation: In the lumbar region, the transverse canal dimension, as represented by the interpediculate distance, should progressively increase from L1 to L5[cite: 88].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. The lateral masses of the sacrum are flat and are anatomically termed the:
questionBank.explanation: The S1 body protrudes anteriorly as the sacral promontory, while the lateral masses are flat and are termed the sacral alae[cite: 89].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, from C2 to C6, the foramen transversarium transmits a plexus of sympathetic nerves, the vertebral vein, and which artery?
questionBank.explanation: Each transverse process possesses a foramen transversarium, which from C2-C6 transmits the vertebral artery and vein, as well as a plexus of sympathetic nerves[cite: 90].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: The facet (zygoapophyseal) joints are innervated by which specific nerve branch?

options.label: A
options.text: Ventral ramus of the mixed spinal nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Medial branch of the dorsal ramus

questionBank.answer: Medial branch of the dorsal ramus
questionBank.explanation: The facet joints are innervated by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of the mixed spinal nerve[cite: 92].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, what normal anatomical variant describes the asymmetry in the sagittal orientation of the facet joints at the same level, occurring most commonly at L4/L5 and L5/S1?
questionBank.explanation: Facet tropism is a normal variant, occurring most commonly at L4/L5 and L5/S1, referring to asymmetry in the sagittal orientation of the facet joints at the same level[cite: 90].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: in adults, why does the vertebral body marrow appear hyperintense relative to the intervertebral disc on T1-weighted MRI?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to a high proportion of yellow (fatty) marrow

options.label: B
options.text: Due to a high proportion of red (haemopoietic) marrow

options.label: C
options.text: Due to calcification of the trabeculae

options.label: D
options.text: Due to increased vascularity in the subchondral bone

questionBank.answer: Due to a high proportion of yellow (fatty) marrow
questionBank.explanation: In adults, the high proportion of yellow marrow results in the marrow appearing hyperintense to the IVD, particularly in the lumbar region[cite: 92].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. At approximately what age does the intervertebral disc become avascular, relying on diffusion through the end-plates for nutrition?
questionBank.explanation: The IVD is avascular by age ~25-30 years, the disc receiving nutrition by diffusion through the end-plates[cite: 93].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, the nucleus pulposus appears hyperintense on T2-weighted MRI primarily due to its high content of what substance?
questionBank.explanation: The NP consists of a gel-like substance with ~90% of its content being water, rendering it hyperintense on T2W images[cite: 93].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: A lumbosacral transitional vertebra (LSTV), often termed 'lumbarization' or 'sacralization', occurs in approximately what percentage of the population?
questionBank.explanation: ...variation in the numbering of the last lumbar vertebra occurs with lumbosacral transitional junctions, occurring in ~16% of the population and also being termed 'lumbarization' or 'sacralization'[cite: 85].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: For radiological anatomy, in a normal adult, what is the standard range for the cervical lordosis curvature?
questionBank.explanation: Four curvatures are seen in the sagittal plane in adults... cervical lordosis; from C1 to T2, ranging from 30 to 40°[cite: 85].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Which option best answers the following anatomical question: the atlas (C1) ring is formed by an anterior arch and two neural arches. By what age do the neural arches typically fuse with the anterior arch?
questionBank.explanation: The neural arches fuse by age 3 years to form the posterior arch and fuse with the anterior arch by age 7 years[cite: 86].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: Select the most accurate answer. In adults, the normal anterior atlanto-dens interval should be less than what measurement?
questionBank.explanation: The normal anterior atlanto-dens interval is <5 mm in children and <3 mm in adults[cite: 87].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: On an anatomy/imaging review, chamberlain's line, used to assess the relationship of the dens to the skull base, runs between the posterior margin of the foramen magnum and which other anatomical landmark?

options.label: A
options.text: The posterior tip of the hard palate

options.label: D
options.text: The anterior arch of the atlas

questionBank.answer: The posterior tip of the hard palate
questionBank.explanation: Chamberlains line; runs between the posterior tip of the hard palate and the posterior margin of the foramen magnum[cite: 87].

questionBank.chapter: The vertebral column and spinal cord
questionBank.question: In the cervical spine, uncinate processes point superiorly from the posterolateral aspects of the superior end-plate to articulate with the vertebra above. What are these joints called?
questionBank.explanation: Two uncinate processes point superiorly from the posterolateral aspects of the superior end-plate to articulate with the inferior end-plate of the vertebra above, forming the neurocentral joints (of Luschka)[cite: 87].
